# What are *Critical AI Literacies*?

- Critical AI Literacies (CAILs) concern the *critical thinking* about AI products, histories, and ecosystems 
- Plural Literac**ies** as they involve different theoretical and practical perspectives on AI
- CAILs concern the knowledge necessary to going beyond the question of *how to use AI* to *when, where and why to use it, and importantly, when NOT to use it*, empowering students (and teachers) to become active decision-makers rather than passive consumers
- "CAILs centre human cognition and uphold the integrity of academic research and education." [@guestsuarezrooij2025], focusing on technical, cognitive, societal and environmental evidence rather than following the claims and promises put forward by the technology industry
- CAILs communicate the knowledge necessary to "tell apart nonsense hype from true theoretical computer scientific claims" (Olivia Guest, https://olivia.science/ai/)


# Terminology "AI"

## **{chatbots + LLM + generative + ANN}** 

Despite common usage of the term "AI", there is no such thing as "the AI". In fact, AI is a very vague term which encompasses many different types of models and applications. 

Here, we focus on what is often referred to as *generative AI*, involving large language models (LLMs) built with Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) and implemented through chatbot interfaces. 
We refer to these models as "GenAI chatbots". Leaving out the AI in "GenAI chatbots", as it is devoid of any information regarding the underlying model and technology, we only end up with *generative* and *chatbots* which, in theory, could also be built based on a simple model (in terms of the number of parameters), such as a "Bernoulli naive Bayes". For the sake of simplicity, we gloss over some of the nuances of the terminology. 

![@guest2025against suggest this cartoon set theoretic view on various terms used when discussing the superset AI](images/ai_overview.png)

Nonetheless, being as specific as possible about a particular application that is considered "AI" is crucial. 
Talking about "the AI" also evokes a mythical image of AI, seeing it as a creature that is difficult to tame and self-acting, where in fact, the "creators", i.e. the companies (and researchers), themselves should be in charge to mitigate any risks accompanied with such systems. Vague terminology further makes obscure the underlying technology, often arousing unwarranted awe about their capabilities in society.

![The terminator, a cyborg assassin from 2029 so watch out once we've reached that year. [source](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0088247/mediaviewer/rm1817347072/)](images/terminator.png)


Simply calling things "an/the AI" impedes making a distinction between useful, ethical applications and unwanted, unethical applications. It even leads people to be "in favour" or "against" AI, when, in fact, such a binary stance may not be appropriate nor desirable. Rather than considering AI either as the doom of society or the solution to all of our problems, talking about different AI systems allows us for a more nuanced discussion about how these systems should be treated, regulated and used in society. The environmental costs of *AI* offers a pertinent example here (see Topic on Environment). There are many ways in which systems that would be considered *AI* help to protect the environemnt, for instance in detecting forest fires early (see description of such projects [here](https://www.hiig.de/en/ai-for-environmental-protection/)). However, these systems are very different in their architectures, electricity and water consumptions and functions from the GenAI chatbot systems we discuss here. Claims that *AI* in general will save our planet if we only invest more and more in it are thus misguided.

# Prerequisites

You should have already acquired a basic knowledge of AI, for example through completing the "Edulabs KI Crashkurs" offered by the University of Cologne (only available in German). 
Regarding, introductions to AI in English, we recommend [The Bullshit Machines](https://thebullshitmachines.com/).

More concretely, you should be familiar with the following concepts: 

1. the difference between deterministic and probabilistic models. 
2. LLMs, chatbots, and combination of both (ChatGPT is not equal to LLM)
3. ...
